blocks.text: CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE KIDNEY AND UROLOGICAL DISORDERS

These disorders result from structural malformation or function of the genitourinary system that may lead to kidney impairment. These disorders include diseases originating from the kidney and systemic diseases, which result in complications affecting the kidney. Hypertension and diabetes mellitus are the commonest conditions causing complications in the kidney; therefore, all patients with hypertension and diabetes mellitus should be regularly screened for kidney complications.

blocks.text: Chronic Kidney Diseases (CKD)

It is structural or functional kidney damage present for >3 months, with or without a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Early screening in high-risk groups [hypertension, Diabetes and glomerular diseases] is crucial in improving the outcome of CKD. Once the cause and plan for care have been established, adults with early CKD stages 1-3 can be managed at the primary care level. Patients with CKD stage 4 should be referred to a nephrologist whenever possible.

Drug Use Principles in CKD
Regularly review all medications and adjust according to eGFR
Use CKD-EPI (adults) and Schwartz equation (children) to estimate eGFR
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs
Check history of drug allergies/adverse reactions before prescribing
Monitor drug toxicity and serum levels where available (e.g. aminoglycosides)
General CKD Management Principles
Reduce proteinuria regardless of blood pressure status
Monitor kidney function and serum potassium closely
Correct volume depletion before starting ACE inhibitors or ARBs to avoid AKI
Identify and treat underlying cause (e.g. diabetes, hypertension, glomerular disease)
Consider nephrology referral for possible kidney biopsy

Hyperlipidemia and Referral to a Nephrologist (CKD)

Hyperlipidemia, when present as a co-existent risk factor in chronic kidney disease (CKD), should be managed according to the relevant cardiovascular guidelines (see Chapter 20 Cardiovascular disease conditions).

blocks.text: Referral to a nephrologist is indicated in the following situations:
Reduced kidney function: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² (CKD stage G3 or worse) or rapid decline in eGFR (>5 mL/min/1.73 m² per year).
Significant albuminuria/proteinuria: Persistent urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) ≥30 mg/g on at least two occasions, nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), or nephrotic syndrome.

blocks.text: Active urinary sediment or unexplained hematuria: Presence of red blood cell casts, dysmorphic red blood cells, or other active sediment.
Suspected or confirmed secondary kidney disease: Including congenital anomalies, glomerulonephritis, and systemic diseases such as lupus nephritis or HIV-associated nephropathy.

blocks.text: CKD complications: Refractory anemia, electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis), or bone mineral disorders not responding to initial therapy.
